entry.title: Camera Safety Area and Camera Dynamics for Top-Down Games
entry.summary: A top-down action game's camera usually has a fixed angle and distance, which falls short in boss fights and big set pieces. Two POV corrections inserted in the PlayerCameraManager: a safe frame that pulls back automatically, and additive camera moves described by curve assets.
entry.content:
A custom PlayerCameraManager, plus two components and a DataAsset, let a top-down camera “automatically keep targets in frame” and “play short camera moves for a performance”. The PER_ prefix in this post is the demo project’s naming, and YOURMODULE_API should be your own module’s; the full source is at the end. ⚠️ Everything below was implemented and verified on UE 5.8. Engine behavior may differ in other versions.

The problem#

A top-down action game’s camera is usually a SpringArm attached to the player, with a fixed angle and a fixed distance. That works for regular combat, but falls short in two situations:

SituationProblemFeature
Boss fights, large enemies, the player knocked far awayImportant targets leave the screen and the player misses attack wind-upsSafe frame: pull back automatically so targets stay on screen
A boss leaps, an ultimate plays, a charged burstShort camera offsets, push-ins, pull-outs and FOV changes tied to the actionCamera Dynamics: describe the move with curve assets; code only plays them

Both features share the same design goals:

  • Don’t touch CameraBoom’s parameters: TargetArmLength and rotation stay as they are, so existing Blueprint camera animations (a death camera, for example) keep working.
  • Only active in the player’s view: automatically disabled when a Level Sequence cutscene takes over, so cutscene cameras are untouched.
  • Designers and artists can tune it themselves: parameters live on components and DataAssets, no code changes needed.

Demo: the safe frame#


The green box is the safe frame. When an enemy nears its edge, the camera pulls back along the view direction, then slowly returns once the enemy is back inside

🎬 If the video doesn’t play: download demo_safe_frame.mp4

Architecture: how one frame of camera is computed#

Both features live on a custom APER_PlayerCameraManager. The key is the insertion point: after the Pawn’s camera component has computed the view (POV), and before the engine’s Camera Modifiers (camera shakes, CineShot) are applied.

flowchart TD A["APER_PlayerCameraManager::UpdateCamera<br/>advance Camera Dynamics playback time"] --> B["Super::UpdateCamera"] B --> C["UpdateViewTargetInternal"] C --> D["Super: Pawn's SpringArm + CameraComponent<br/>compute the base POV"] D --> E{"Is the ViewTarget the player Pawn?"} E -- No (cutscene) --> H E -- Yes --> F["① Safe frame<br/>UPER_CameraFramingComponent::ApplyFraming<br/>pull back along the view direction"] F --> G["② Camera Dynamics<br/>apply each active effect in order"] G --> H["Engine Camera Modifiers<br/>(camera shakes, etc.)"] H --> I["Final view"]

Why this insertion point?

  • After the Pawn’s camera: we get the “normal” view and only need to apply a delta, instead of rewriting the whole camera logic.
  • Before Camera Modifiers: camera shakes stack on top last, so the safe frame’s pull-back doesn’t swallow them, and they don’t affect the safe frame’s math.
  • Checking OutVT.Target != Pawn: when a Level Sequence plays, the ViewTarget switches to the cutscene camera and both features turn off on their own.

Safe frame (Camera Framing)#

Who does what#

ClassAttached toResponsibility
UPER_CameraTargetComponentEnemies, bosses, or any Actor that needs to stay in frameMarks “this point must stay on screen”
UPER_CameraFramingComponentThe playerComputes how far to pull back each frame
APER_PlayerCameraManagerSet on the PlayerControllerCalls ApplyFraming

UPER_CameraTargetComponent is a USceneComponent, so in the character Blueprint you can attach it to a socket or adjust its height. It is disabled by default; enable it in Details, or call this from Blueprint when needed (for example when a boss fight starts):

There is also MaxFramingDistance: targets farther than this from the player are ignored for now, so an enemy on the other side of the map can’t drag the camera all the way out.

The core math: solve for “how far back” directly#

The intuitive approach is “if a target is outside the frame, back up a little until it’s inside”, but that jitters back and forth and takes several frames to converge. Instead, we solve the exact pull-back distance every frame.

Let the camera position be CCC and its forward, right and up axes be F^,R^,U^\hat{F}, \hat{R}, \hat{U}F^,R^,U^. For a target point TTT:

depth=(T−C)⋅F^,side=∣(T−C)⋅R^∣,vertical=∣(T−C)⋅U^∣\text{depth} = (T - C)\cdot\hat{F},\quad \text{side} = |(T - C)\cdot\hat{R}|,\quad \text{vertical} = |(T - C)\cdot\hat{U}|depth=(T−C)⋅F^,side=∣(T−C)⋅R^∣,vertical=∣(T−C)⋅U^∣

Under perspective projection, the target’s horizontal position on screen (with half the screen width as 1) is:

xscreen=sidedepth⋅tan⁡(θH)x_{screen} = \frac{\text{side}}{\text{depth} \cdot \tan(\theta_H)}xscreen​=depth⋅tan(θH​)side​

Moving the camera back by DDD along the view direction makes the depth depth+D\text{depth} + Ddepth+D while the side distance stays the same. For the target to fall inside the safe frame (with width ratio www):

side(depth+D)tan⁡(θH)≤w⟹D≥sidew⋅tan⁡(θH)−depth\frac{\text{side}}{(\text{depth} + D)\tan(\theta_H)} \le w \quad\Longrightarrow\quad D \ge \frac{\text{side}}{w \cdot \tan(\theta_H)} - \text{depth}(depth+D)tan(θH​)side​≤w⟹D≥w⋅tan(θH​)side​−depth

The vertical axis works the same way. The maximum over all targets and both axes is the pull-back this frame needs:

Why only pull back along the view direction? The camera’s orientation doesn’t change, so the player always stays at the center of the screen and controls feel the same while zoomed out. Visually it’s the same as lengthening the SpringArm, without touching the SpringArm itself.

Getting the correct tangent of the half-FOV#

You can’t just use POV.FOV: UE’s FOV is horizontal by default, but the viewport aspect ratio and the AspectRatioAxisConstraint setting both affect the actual vertical FOV, and converting it yourself is easy to get wrong.

Instead we read the projection matrix the engine actually renders with:

However the window is resized and whichever axis locks the FOV, the result matches the screen. The cost is that it’s last frame’s projection, so it lags one frame when the FOV changes sharply, which isn’t noticeable in practice.

Pull out fast, pull back in slowly#

  • Pull out faster (default 4): when a target is about to leave the frame, react immediately or the player will miss the attack.
  • Pull back in slower (default 1.5): once targets are back inside, return gently so an enemy hovering at the edge doesn’t make the camera pump in and out.
  • MaxPullBackDistance cap: stops the camera from pulling back forever when a target is too far away.

Parameters#

UPER_CameraFramingComponent (player)

ParameterDefaultDescription
SafeFrameWidthRatio0.8Safe frame width as a fraction of the screen; outside it is the no-go zone
SafeFrameHeightRatio0.7Safe frame height as a fraction of the screen
MaxPullBackDistance2000Maximum pull-back distance (cm)
PullOutSpeed4Interpolation speed when pulling out
PullInSpeed1.5Interpolation speed when pulling back in

UPER_CameraTargetComponent (target)

ParameterDefaultDescription
bCameraTargetActivefalseWhether this target counts for the safe frame
MaxFramingDistance0Ignored when farther than this from the player; 0 means no limit

Debug display#

In the console:

The screen shows:

  • A green rectangle: the safe frame
  • Each active target: green inside the frame, red outside, labeled with the Actor name
  • Text: current / required / maximum pull-back, target count, tangent of the half-FOV and other solver inputs

The debug code is wrapped in #if ENABLE_DRAW_DEBUG, so Shipping builds compile it out entirely.

Walkthrough: the safe frame#


The full flow: adding the components, enabling targets, and setting the CameraManager

🎬 If the video doesn’t play: download setup_safe_frame.mp4

1. Player: tune the safe frame

On the player character’s CameraFramingComponent, adjust the frame size and pull speeds under the Camera category in Details.

2. Targets: add a CameraTarget and enable it

Add a CameraTargetComponent to an enemy (or any Actor that needs to stay in frame); you can attach it to a socket on the Mesh to set its height. There are two ways to enable it: tick Camera Target Active in Details, or call Set Camera Target Active from Blueprint (for example, on when a boss fight starts and off when it ends).

3. Set the CameraManager

In the PlayerController’s Class Defaults, set Player Camera Manager Class to PER_PlayerCameraManager. A C++ Controller can also set it in its constructor:

If the Controller Blueprint’s Class Defaults override it, change it back, or neither feature will run.

4. Check the result

In PIE, enter PER.ShowCameraSafeFrame 1 in the console and check that the frame size and pull-back distance look right.

Camera Dynamics (additive camera moves)#


Creating a Camera Dynamics Data asset, editing its curves, and playing it on jump

🎬 If the video doesn’t play: download camera_dynamics.mp4

Data layout#

A camera move is a DataAsset holding several “effect entries”, each describing a change over time with curves:

EffectWhat it doesTypical use
Position OffsetOffsets the camera position, in world space or camera space (X forward, Y right, Z up)Camera rises with a leaping boss
Arm DistancePulls out (positive) or pushes in (negative) along the view, same as changing arm lengthPush in before an ultimate, pull out on the burst
FOVAdds/subtracts FOV (degrees), clamped to 1–170Sense of speed for dashes and charged bursts

There’s no separate length field: the duration is the time of the last key across all curves.

Extensible effect entries#

The effect base class is declared EditInlineNew + DefaultToInstanced, so entries can be added and edited from a dropdown right in the DataAsset’s array:

To add a new kind of effect (roll, depth of field, …), subclass it and implement the two functions; the CameraManager doesn’t change. FOV as an example:

Playing and stopping#

Blueprint or C++ calls static functions directly, no need to fetch the CameraManager first:

Calling the same Data repeatedly stacks: two impacts in a row play two copies of the effect at once.

Active state and weight#

Each playing effect is stored as one record:

The weight is the minimum of three blends, then SmoothStep softens the start and end:

Looping effects sample at Fmod(Elapsed, Duration), so the curves replay from the start.

Where should time advance?#

This is the easiest part to get wrong. The intuitive place is UpdateViewTargetInternal, but while blending between ViewTargets, the engine calls it twice per frame (once for the old target, once for the new), so time runs at double speed.

So advancing time and removing expired entries happen in UpdateCamera, which runs once per frame:

UpdateViewTargetInternal only reads the time to apply effects, so however many times it’s called, the result is the same.

Example: boss jump#

  1. In the Content Browser, create a Data Asset of class PER_CameraDynamicsData and name it CD_BossJump.
  2. Add a Position Offset to Modifiers, set Space to World, and key the Z curve: 0 s → 0, 0.4 s → 150, 1.0 s → 0.
  3. Add an Arm Distance: 0 s → 0, 0.4 s → 300, 1.0 s → 0.
  4. BlendInTime = 0.1, BlendOutTime = 0.2.
  5. Call AddCameraDynamics(CD_BossJump) from the boss jump animation’s AnimNotify or from the ability.

Full source#

The full source of the Camera/ folder. Replace YOURMODULE_API with your module’s API macro; UE_LOG uses LogTemp, which you can swap for your project’s own log category.

PER_PlayerCameraManager.h#

PER_PlayerCameraManager.cpp#

PER_CameraFramingComponent.h#

PER_CameraFramingComponent.cpp#

PER_CameraTargetComponent.h#

PER_CameraTargetComponent.cpp#

PER_CameraDynamicsData.h#

PER_CameraDynamicsData.cpp#

Player, AI character and Controller (added lines)#

Add the safe frame component in the player character’s constructor:

Add the target point in the AI character’s constructor (at the capsule center by default):

Set the CameraManager in the PlayerController’s constructor:

Design decisions and pitfalls#

DecisionWhy
Modify the POV, not the SpringArmBlueprint camera animations and the SpringArm’s collision and lag all keep working; both features are purely additive
The safe frame only pulls back along the viewThe player stays centered and control directions don’t change; the math can be solved directly instead of iterated
Tangent of the half-FOV from the projection matrixMatches the aspect ratio and FOV axis lock automatically, no manual conversion
Pull out fast, pull back in slowlyThreats aren’t missed, and the camera doesn’t jitter when a target sits at the edge
Targets disabled by defaultRegular mobs don’t move the camera; only moments that call for it opt in
Time advances in UpdateCameraUpdateViewTargetInternal runs twice per frame during ViewTarget blends
Effects as Instanced UObjectsNew effect types don’t touch the player; designers combine several effects in one asset
Both disabled during cutscenesChecked with ViewTarget != Pawn, no extra flags or state

Known limitations#

  • Perspective projection only: the safe frame is skipped for orthographic projection (ProjectionMode != Perspective returns early).
  • Targets are found with TObjectIterator: fine with a few targets; with many on screen, register components to a UWorldSubsystem in BeginPlay / EndPlay instead.
  • Projection data is from last frame: when the FOV changes sharply (for example an instant jump from an FOV effect), the safe frame reacts one frame late.

entry.title: Niagara as an AnimNotifyState: Effects That Follow Attack Animations, and the SetUsingAbsoluteLocation Gotcha
entry.summary: Slash and trail effects on attack animations often need to follow the weapon at first and then stay behind when they end. How to wrap Niagara in an AnimNotifyState, and the UpdateComponentToWorld gotcha I hit when stopping the follow midway.
entry.content:
One AnimNotifyState that spawns, follows and releases a Niagara effect during a set range of an attack animation, and also respects the character’s hit-stop (TimeDilation). In the code below, replace YOURMODULE_API with your own project’s module name. ⚠️ Everything here was implemented and tested on UE 5.6. Newer engine versions may behave differently.

Requirements#

Effects in attack animations (slashes, trails, charge-up glows) usually need to:

  • Appear during a specific range of the animation, adjustable by dragging the Notify range on the Montage / AnimSequence
  • Spawn on a Socket, with optional offset, rotation and scale
  • Decide separately whether location and rotation follow the character (for example, follow location but not rotation)
  • When the Notify ends, either disappear immediately or stay where they are and finish playing
  • Slow down along with the character during hit-stop (when CustomTimeDilation drops)

The engine’s built-in Timed Niagara Effect covers part of this, but “stop following midway” and “respect TimeDilation” have to be built yourself. So I wrote my own AnimNotifyState and exposed parameters, so teammates and combat designers can tune the effect freely.

Spawn and attach#

Spawn the effect attached directly to a Socket on the Mesh:

KeepRelativeOffset treats LocationOffset / RotationOffset as offsets relative to the Socket.

Stop following midway: use Absolute, not Detach#

When you want the effect to stop following the character, the first instinct is DetachFromComponent. Here I use Absolute Location / Rotation instead: the component stays attached to the Mesh, it just stops inheriting location or rotation from its parent.

The benefits:

  • Location and rotation can be controlled separately (Detach cuts everything at once)
  • The attachment doesn’t change, so the component’s lifetime still follows the character

Gotcha: always call UpdateComponentToWorld after SetUsingAbsoluteLocation#

I called only SetUsingAbsoluteLocation(true), then SetWorldLocation(...), and the effect ended up in the wrong place. Every transform call after that, such as SetWorldLocation and SetWorldRotation, goes wrong.

The reason is in how SetAbsolute is implemented:

After changing the flags, SetAbsolute calls UpdateComponentToWorld() internally. Calling SetUsingAbsoluteLocation / SetUsingAbsoluteRotation on their own does not.

So when you use them on their own, add the call yourself:

My understanding (a guess): the flag changes, but the component’s cached ComponentToWorld is still the old one, so later transform math is built on stale data.

If you’re setting location, rotation and scale all at once, SetAbsolute is simplest. To change just one of them, pass the current values for the other two:

Making the effect respect hit-stop TimeDilation#

By default, Niagara ignores the Actor’s CustomTimeDilation. Here’s how to make it respect it:

  • SetForceSolo(true): stops this component from being batch-simulated with other instances of the same system, which is what lets CustomTimeDilation take effect
  • The character’s CustomTimeDilation keeps changing during hit-stop, so sync it every frame in NotifyTick
  • In NotifyEnd, set TimeDilation back to 1.0, so an effect left behind to finish playing doesn’t stay in slow motion

Editor preview#

When previewing in the animation editor, World->IsPreviewWorld() is true. In that case it just spawns the effect so artists can check its placement, and skips TimeDilation and state tracking, so it doesn’t break when the preview world has no character or related data.

Gotcha 2: the Notify object is shared by every character#

An AnimNotifyState object lives on the animation asset, so every character playing that animation shares the same instance. Characters don’t each get their own copy.

If you store the spawned effect in a single member variable, things break when two characters play the same animation at the same time (for example, two of the same enemy attacking together):

  1. The second character’s NotifyBegin overwrites the first character’s effect pointer
  2. The first character’s NotifyEnd then clears the pointer
  3. The second character’s effect never gets its NotifyEnd: it never stops following, and its TimeDilation stays stuck in slow motion

So use a Map instead, keyed by MeshComp, to track each character’s effect separately:

  • TWeakObjectPtr means no dangling pointers when a character or effect is destroyed
  • NotifyEnd removes that Mesh’s entry; NotifyBegin also cleans up any stale entries

Full source#

NiagaraFreezeFrame_AnimNotifyState.h#

NiagaraFreezeFrame_AnimNotifyState.cpp#

Summary#

  • Make attack effects an AnimNotifyState, so animators can adjust when they appear directly on the animation
  • To stop following midway, use Absolute Location / Rotation, which lets you control location and rotation separately
  • After calling SetUsingAbsoluteLocation / SetUsingAbsoluteRotation on their own, add UpdateComponentToWorld(), or use SetAbsolute, which updates automatically
  • To respect hit-stop, use SetForceSolo(true) and sync SetCustomTimeDilation every frame
  • The Notify object is shared by every character, so track each character’s effect in a Map keyed by MeshComp

Reminder: all of this is UE 5.6 behavior. Check it yourself on other versions.

entry.title: Axis-Snap Movement for Top-Down Games: Letting the Keyboard Follow the Stairs
entry.summary: In a top-down game, the keyboard can only input 8 directions (up, down, left, right and 4 diagonals). When a diagonal staircase, a narrow bridge or a winding walkway doesn't line up with any of those 8 directions...
entry.content:
One Volume plus a few functions on the player side fix 8-direction keyboard movement on diagonal and curved paths. In the code below, replace YOURMODULE_API and AMyPlayerCharacter with the names from your own project.

The problem#

In a top-down game, the keyboard can only input 8 directions (up, down, left, right and 4 diagonals). When the level has diagonal stairs, narrow bridges or winding walkways that don’t line up with any of those 8 directions:

  • The player has to keep switching between two direction keys to zigzag along the path
  • It’s easy to bump into walls, get stuck on railings, or fall off the side of a bridge

Gamepads don’t have this problem: an analog stick can point at any angle.

The idea#

Place a Volume over these sections and give it a snap axis (the direction the path runs). While the player moves with the keyboard inside the Volume, any input that points roughly along the path gets snapped onto the snap axis.

Design goals:

  • Keyboard only: gamepads are unaffected
  • The snap axis is bidirectional: walking back snaps to the opposite direction automatically, so you don’t need a second Volume
  • Angle threshold: input beyond SnapAngle is left untouched, so the player can still leave the path (for example, stepping sideways off the stairs)
  • Smooth transitions: no sudden turns when entering, leaving or switching between Volumes
  • Only the input direction changes; the character isn’t moved directly, so collision, speed and Root Motion all work as before

Demo#


Using only the arrow keys, the character walks up the diagonal stairs and turns onto the bridge

🎬 If the video doesn’t play: download demo_stairs.mp4

Without snapping, the stairs run halfway between two direction keys, so the player has to keep alternating keys, zigzags, and easily hits the railings. With the snap Volume, holding one key roughly toward the stairs keeps the character steadily on the stairs’ center line.

Architecture#

Technique 1: Build one Volume out of several shapes#

A curved staircase is hard to cover with a single Box. Instead, the Volume can combine any number of shapes, and you can adjust them directly in the editor.

Shape settings you can edit inline in the Details panel#

Each shape setting is a UObject marked with:

Declare them as an array with UPROPERTY(EditAnywhere, Instanced), and the Details panel lets you pick Box / Sphere / Capsule from a dropdown and expand its parameters in place, with no extra assets.

Each shape setting does only three things: create the matching ShapeComponent, apply its parameters to that component, and return its type name.

Generate components from the settings#

Rebuild the shape components in OnConstruction, so dragging or editing properties updates them right away:

  • Component names follow the pattern GuideShape_<Type>_<Index>
  • A component with that name already exists → only update its parameters, don’t recreate it
  • It doesn’t exist → create it with NewObject, then AddInstanceComponent and RegisterComponent
  • Old components whose settings were removed → unbind them and destroy them

Gotcha: when you change a parameter of an element inside the array, the engine doesn’t rerun the Construction Script. Override PostEditChangeChainProperty, and call RerunConstructionScripts() when the change comes from ShapeConfigs.

Merge several shapes into one Volume#

Each shape fires its own Begin / End Overlap. When the player walks from one Box into a connected Box, they get “left A” and “entered B”. If you forwarded those directly, the player would keep entering and leaving while still inside the Volume.

The fix is an overlap count:

  • Count goes 0 → 1: only then does it count as “entered the Volume”
  • Count goes 1 → 0: only then does it count as “left the Volume”

Other details#

  • Set the shape components explicitly to the Trigger collision profile and enable GenerateOverlapEvents
  • Bind events with AddUniqueDynamic, and don’t call Clear() first, or you’ll wipe out bindings from other systems
  • Enable bGenerateOverlapEventsDuringLevelStreaming, so a Volume in a streamed level still fires “enter” if the player is already standing in it when it loads
  • On EndPlay (for example when a streamed level unloads), send “exit” yourself to every Actor still inside, so the player isn’t left inside a Volume that no longer exists
  • Before rebuilding shapes at runtime, also send “exit” first; otherwise the counts are cleared and the “exit” never arrives

Technique 2: Getting the snap axis#

ModeSnap axis sourceUse for
ArrowThe arrow component’s forward vectorStraight stairs, bridges
SplineThe spline’s tangent at the point closest to the playerCurved sections

Both are flattened onto the horizontal plane (GetSafeNormal2D), keeping only the direction. In Spline mode the snap direction changes continuously with the player’s position, so it naturally follows the curve. If the spline has too few points or the tangent is invalid, it falls back to the arrow direction.

Technique 3: The snap calculation#

  • Add a tiny tolerance (0.01°) when comparing angles, so input right on the boundary doesn’t flicker between snapping and not snapping because of floating-point error
  • The snapped direction is also written back as the “last input direction”, so abilities like dodge also follow the snapped direction

Technique 4: Smooth transitions#

If the direction snapped instantly on entering the Volume, the character would turn abruptly and feel bad. There are two kinds of transitions here:

Weight transition#

  • Entering the first Volume: weight goes 0 → 1
  • Leaving all Volumes: weight goes 1 → 0
  • The transition takes MovementGuideBlendTime (default 0.1 s; 0 means instant)
  • While fading out after leaving, the last snap axis keeps being used

The weight isn’t accumulated on Tick. Instead it stores the start value, the target value and the start time, and computes the current value from the world time when needed. The logic stays simple and no error builds up.

Snap axis transition#

When two Volumes touch or overlap, the snap axis can change suddenly. On a switch, store the old axis and the start time, then interpolate from the old axis to the new one over the transition time.

Because the axis is bidirectional, flip the old axis to the same side as the new one before interpolating, or it will swing the long way around.

Overlapping Volumes#

The player keeps a list of the Volumes it’s in, and the last one entered wins. When it leaves the active Volume, the previous Volume it’s still inside takes over. Overlaps usually mean something was placed wrong, so it also logs a warning.

Full source#

MyMovementGuideVolume.h#

MyMovementGuideVolume.cpp#

PlayerCharacter.h (additions)#

Replace AMyPlayerCharacter with your player class name (and change the class cast in the Volume’s .cpp too).

PlayerCharacter.cpp (additions)#

The call in Move()#

Walkthrough: placing a snap Volume on diagonal stairs#


Full recording: place the Volume → set the shape and snap mode → align the arrow → test in game

🎬 If the video doesn’t play: download setup_walkthrough.mp4

Here are the steps from the recording:

1. Drag the Volume into the level

2. Set the shape and snap mode

  • Add a Box to ShapeConfigs and adjust BoxExtent so the Volume covers the whole staircase (the full width of the walkway, from the bottom step to the top)
  • Set GuideMode to Arrow (straight stairs)
  • Start with a SnapAngle of 30°

3. Rotate the Actor so the arrow follows the stairs

  • The Volume and the arrow rotate together, so the Box lines up with the stairs too
  • Only the horizontal direction matters: the arrow’s pitch is ignored because the calculation flattens it onto the horizontal plane

4. Check from another angle

5. Test in game

Walk up from the bottom of the stairs with the keyboard, holding one key roughly toward the stairs. The character should move steadily along the stairs (as in the Demo section above). If it feels too sticky, lower SnapAngle; if it doesn’t snap, raise it.

Curved paths#

  1. Change GuideMode to Spline (the editor hides the arrow and shows the spline automatically)
  2. Place spline points along the path’s center line, at least 2
  3. Build the curve out of several Boxes in ShapeConfigs, using each one’s RelativeTransform to set its position and rotation

Tuning tips and caveats#

  • If SnapAngle is too large, it’s hard for the player to leave the path; too small and it won’t snap. Around 30° is a good starting point
  • Avoid overlapping Volumes. When they overlap, the one entered last wins and a warning is logged
  • Only player classes the Volume can cast to get snapped
  • Only the input direction changes, so character collision, movement speed and Root Motion are unaffected

entry.title: UPROPERTY / UFUNCTION Specifier Cheat Sheet
entry.summary: The UPROPERTY and UFUNCTION specifiers I use most in UE C++, and how they differ when exposed to Blueprint.
entry.content:
Why reflection specifiers matter#

UE’s reflection system (UHT) scans macros such as UPROPERTY and UFUNCTION and generates the code needed for serialization, garbage collection and Blueprint exposure. A UObject* pointer without UPROPERTY is not tracked by the GC, so the object can be collected and leave a dangling pointer.

Common UPROPERTY combinations#

SpecifierEffect
EditAnywhereEditable in both Defaults and Instances
EditDefaultsOnlyEditable only in Blueprint Class Defaults
VisibleAnywhereShown but not editable (common for Component pointers)
BlueprintReadOnly / BlueprintReadWriteAccess level in Blueprint graphs
TransientNot serialized; not kept when saving or duplicating the asset
Replicated / ReplicatedUsing=OnRep_XNetwork replication
TIP

Component pointers usually use VisibleAnywhere, BlueprintReadOnly. You can still tweak the component’s own properties in Details, but the pointer itself can’t be swapped out.

Common UFUNCTION combinations#

WARNING

The C++ implementation of a BlueprintNativeEvent must be named FunctionName_Implementation. Always call the original name (or Execute_ for interfaces), never _Implementation directly, or you’ll skip the Blueprint override.

entry.title: GAS Basics: Should the ASC Live on the Pawn or the PlayerState?
entry.summary: The most common choice when setting up the Gameplay Ability System: which actor owns the AbilitySystemComponent, and when to call InitAbilityActorInfo.
entry.content:
Comparing the two options#

On the PawnOn the PlayerState
Character death and respawnAttributes and Effects disappear with the PawnKept on the PlayerState
Good forAI enemies, single-player gamesPlayer characters, multiplayer games
Network update rateSame as the PawnRaise the PlayerState’s NetUpdateFrequency

Initializing when the ASC is on the PlayerState#

The Owner is the PlayerState and the Avatar is the Pawn. The server and the client have to call InitAbilityActorInfo at different times:

NOTE

ASC Replication Mode: player characters usually use Mixed, and AI uses Minimal.
